https://www.dw.com/en/berlin-s-russian-h.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/4wSVN The Russian House has been a fixture on Berlin's Friedrichstrasse since 1984 Image: Schoening/picture alliance Advertisement The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations , it is the subject of fierce disagreements and has long been a bone of contention in Berlin . The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state , its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore. But now, more than 40 years later, French authorities have linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services. "In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations , the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin earlier this week. In response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, Giese emphasized that there are two bilateral agreements between Germany and Russia regarding real estate matters that cannot be easily revoked. "It is, so to speak, an agreement that governs both the Russian House here in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut that we operate in Moscow," Giese said. Any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other. German tax money for Russian propaganda? The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad and International Humanitarian Cooperation. Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany. Since 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine , the agency has been on the EU sanctions list. At the time, the EU justified this by stating that the agency's goal was to consolidate "a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian." Moscow still maintains that the Russian House is a place to celebrate the friendship between the two countries: "The Russian House is Russia's cultural embassy in the heart of Berlin," according to the Russian Embassy's website. The events that take place there attract 200,000 visitors a year, according to Russian House organizers. Critics label them as propaganda. Symbols of friendship remained on display in Berlin's Russian House in October 2023, more than year after the Russian invasion of Ukraine Image: Dmyrto Katkov/DW Berlin media outlets have repeatedly reported on events at the in-house cinema where, for example, a Holocaust film was shown in which Ukrainian citizens were portrayed as Nazis . In an interview in August 2025, Robin Wagener, a member of the Bundestag for the opposition Green Party , told DW: "It is time we recognized that this is not mutual cultural exchange, but Russian war propaganda in Germany." Germany fears closure of Goethe-Institut in Moscow The Russian House is owned by the Russian Federation, but the Federal Republic of Germany pays the property tax for the building on the basis of its legal obligation under the bilateral German-Russian agreement on property issues relating to cultural institutes. Moscow and Berlin are also bound by the Intergovernmental Agreement on Cultural Cooperation, which was signed in December 1992 and entered into force in May 1993. It has a term of five years and is automatically extended for the same period unless one of the parties notifies the other at least six months before the expiration of the respective term. Both agreements — regarding the property of the Russian House and the Goethe-Institut, as well as the cultural cooperation between Russia and Germany — remain in force even in the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine. It is an open secret that the German government is shying away from conflict over the Russian House because it fears the Russian government could respond by closing the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. The institute was already forced to significantly scale back its operations in Russia in May 2023, when restrictions were imposed on the number of German officials in Russia. A few weeks earlier, the Goethe-Institut's bank accounts in Russia were frozen in retaliation after the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office opened a preliminary investigation against the Russian House for violating sanctions and ordered the freeze of its accounts. Berlin detains German-Ukrainian woman for Russian espionage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video So far, the Goethe-Institut continues to offer digital language courses in Russia. The libraries at its branches in Moscow and St. Petersburg continue to receive the latest German literature despite logistical difficulties, as representatives of the institute assured DW earlier this year. Direct Russian-German contacts have become virtually impossible According the cultural agreement, the contracting parties welcome "direct contacts between social groups and associations, including trade unions, churches, religious communities, artists' associations and political, cultural and other foundations." However, in recent years, several German foundations in Russia have been classified as "undesirable organizations." This includes the foundations run by Germany's established political parties. Anyone who cooperates with "undesirable organizations" faces criminal prosecution in Russia. This makes all direct contact provided for in the cultural agreement virtually impossible. This article was originally written in German and first published in August 2025. It was updated and republished in August 2026 to reflect news developments. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters Coles Coles investigates cyber-attack and apologises to customers Supermarket giant says no customer, team or supplier data compromised but recommends customers update passwords Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press Sun 15 Nov 2026 19.25 EST Last modified on Sun 15 Nov 2026 21.49 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised. Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts. “Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident,” the company said in a statement to the stock exchange. Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why? Read more “We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles’ systems. “Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online.” Coles apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at “a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world”. “We have security measures in place to protect customer and supplier accounts and are continuing to closely monitor our system,” it said. “We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reuse the same password across multiple services.” Coles also warned customers to be cautious if they received unexpected emails or SMS messages purporting to be from the retailer, and not to click any links. http://www.bgnes.com/politics/world-lead.text: BGNES Politics World Leaders React to Democrats' Victory in US Midterm Elections World Leaders React to Democrats' Victory in US Midterm Elections 04.11.2026 - 16:30 Share BGNES Former US President Barack Obama welcomed the Democratic victory. Governments and politicians around the world have reacted to the Democratic Party's victory in the US midterm elections, a result that could have major implications for global trade, security and energy prices. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez wrote on X: "Yesterday, the American people voted against policies that only serve to impoverish people. Against hatred. Against sexism. Against climate denial and against the privileges of the elites. "It happened in Brazil. It has just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain." Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere described the result as "a powerful political signal of a change in direction among American voters." "Voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to our positions than those of the president and his administration, for example on climate and the environment, foreign policy and development aid policy," he said. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told reporters that the results would "mark the beginning of a new era in international relations." "We have seen the Democrats take control of the Senate and the House of Representatives, and the American people have expressed their will," he stressed. Greek government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis told SKAI television that relations between Greece and the United States would remain stable. "Greek-American relations will remain strong. The United States is our strategic ally, and this will continue in terms of major projects and all important agreements. Nothing will be affected by this result. Obviously, we respect every election result. The conclusions are clear. "I can also say that it appears there will be people on key committees with whom the Greek government maintains very good relations, and that is important for the country," Marinakis said. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov urged observers to wait for the final results. "Let us wait for the final results. The Democratic Party leadership's approach to relations with Russia is sharply negative. There is nothing new about that. "Our principled and consistent position on Ukraine, as well as our foreign policy in general, is not based on short-term considerations and, naturally, does not depend on fluctuations in the political barometer in other countries. We will continue our work in accordance with the instructions of the President of the Russian Federation," he said, according to RIA Novosti. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told BFM television that much would depend on US President Donald Trump's response to the election results. "Either he will decide to rise above the confrontation, recognising that changes are needed, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly affect people, and I would add that he will limit his international involvement, or he will not. Frankly, that is something we will have to watch over the coming days," Lescure said. Alice Weidel, co-leader of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, told T-Online: "Trump had promised his voters that he would not pursue an interventionist foreign policy... That broken promise is now coming back to haunt the Republicans." Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis described the Democratic victory as sweeping. "I think the result was expected, although the Democrats' victory is, of course, enormous. Even the Republican stronghold of Texas fell, and in some places the Democrats made gains after decades. "In my opinion, this means that until the end of President Trump's term, everything will revolve around impeachment and vetoes, as well as a certain kind of paralysis. On the other hand, President Trump will almost certainly continue doing exactly what he wants. Let us hope that he finally returns to his promise to end the war in Ukraine and resolve the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz," Babis said. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X: "Americans said NO TO WAR, and we support that message. If the US government betrays the will of its people to serve international patrons and blackmailers, it will discover that our NO comes with a nightmare." Jordan Bardella, president of France's far-right opposition National Rally party, stressed the importance of respecting election results. "I am not American, and I am not a voter in the United States. Therefore, we must respect the verdict of the ballot box, including the results of these midterm elections, which, incidentally, are almost always unfavourable to the sitting president. "What is certain is that Donald Trump's second term differs quite significantly in its philosophy and foreign policy from his first, when his political ambition was to withdraw the United States from major global conflicts. "American intervention in Iran has very serious consequences, in my view, not only for the American economy but also for the European economy, particularly for the purchasing power of our citizens given the rise in oil prices. So yes, there is certainly a connection," Bardella said. Former US President Barack Obama welcomed the Democratic victory. "Tonight, the American people sent a clear message - they want politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face. "These results were only possible because extraordinary candidates entered the race in every region of the country, including areas previously considered long shots. They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political views, but they were united by shared values, a belief in public service and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first. "Although this administration still has two years in office, our task now is to roll up our sleeves, make changes wherever we have the authority, prevent further damage and lay the foundations for the future," Obama wrote on X. | BGNES Follow us also on Watch and Comment news Comment in X More from Politics Croatia demands progress on wartime missing persons 18.11.2026 -
